{{italic title}}
'''''Mathematical Excursions: Side Trips along Paths Not Generally Traveled in Elementary Courses in Mathematics''''' is a book on [[popular mathematics]]. It was written by [[Helen Abbot Merrill]], published in 1933 by the Norwood Press,{{r|mt1|amm|mt2|jsh|mg}} and reprinted (posthumously) by [[Dover Publications]] in 1957.{{r|mt3|sprague}}

==Topics==
The book is devoted to mathematical puzzles and pastimes,{{r|mt3}} gathered from Merrill's experience as a teacher.{{r|mt1|mt2}} It has 15 chapters,{{r|jsh}} most on arithmetic and [[number theory]] but with one on geometry.{{r|mt3}}

Its topics include 
[[squared triangular number]]s and other [[Faulhaber's formula|sums of powers]],{{r|mg}} [[Russian peasant multiplication]],{{r|amm}} [[binary number]]s,{{r|amm|mt3}} [[repeating decimal]]s,{{r|amm}} [[magic square]]s,{{r|jsh}} the [[Proof that π is irrational|irrationality of {{pi}}]],{{r|amm|mg}} [[Linkage (mechanical)|mechanical linkages]], linear [[Diophantine equation]]s, the [[15 puzzle]],{{r|mt3}} [[perfect number]]s,{{r|sprague}} and some unsolved problems in number theory.{{r|amm|mg|mt3}}

==Audience and reception==
The book is written for a general audience,{{r|mt1}} and is intended to spark the interest of high school students in mathematics.{{r|jsh}}
In general, only high school levels of algebra and geometry are needed to appreciate the book and solve its problems.{{r|mt1}}
It could be used as individual reading, or in mathematics clubs,{{r|amm}}
and also for mathematics teachers looking for examples and demonstrations for their classes.{{r|mg}}

Of the original edition, reviewer [[David Eugene Smith]] wrote "the book ought to be in the hands of all teachers and on the shelves of all high schools and colleges".{{r|mt2}} By the time of the 1957 reprint, reviewer [[Samuel L. Greitzer]] complained about its obsolete notation, as well as its uneven level of exposition and non-uniform inclusion of solutions to problems,{{r|mt3}} and reviewer [[Roland Sprague]] noted that its treatment of [[perfect number]]s was out of date.{{r|sprague}} Nevertheless, Greitzer suggested that it would be an appropriate supplement in [[mathematics education]] at the [[secondary education|secondary level]].{{r|mt3}}
